output.query: congenital long QT syndrome syncope diagnosis and management

results.key_finding: LQTS is diagnosed with a QTc of 480 ms or more on repeated 12-lead ECGs, or an LQTS risk score above 3. Beta-blockers, preferably non-selective (nadolol or propranolol), are recommended in patients with documented QT prolongation; QT-prolonging drugs are avoided and electrolyte abnormalities corrected. An ICD is recommended after cardiac arrest, and for arrhythmic syncope or haemodynamically not tolerated ventricular arrhythmia despite beta-blocker therapy; left cardiac sympathetic denervation is an option. Genetic testing and cascade screening of relatives are recommended.
results.title: 2022 ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death (Zeppenfeld K et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126)

results.key_finding: Myoclonic jerks lasting seconds are common during syncope and do not by themselves indicate epilepsy; syncope during exertion is a high-risk feature.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: LQT1 (KCNQ1 mutation, IKs current loss) is the most common LQTS subtype and is specifically triggered by exercise and emotional arousal due to adrenergic QT maladaptation; swimming is a classic trigger because it combines immersion (adrenergic response) with exercise
Patients with LQTS are frequently first labelled as having epilepsy; a 12-lead ECG belongs in the evaluation of every first 'seizure'.
Drowning in a young adult without clear head trauma or intoxication should prompt ECG-based cardiac channelopathy screening in all surviving relatives
Paradoxical QTc prolongation during exercise stress testing (failure to shorten normally) is a supporting diagnostic finding for LQT1 and can be captured before genetic confirmation
A QTc of 500 ms or more marks higher arrhythmic risk in congenital LQTS; non-selective beta-blockade and avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs are first-line.
diagnostic_traps: Prior epilepsy label with antiepileptic on the medication list strongly anchors clinicians to the seizure framework
Witnessed convulsive movements prompt neurology referral and AED prescription without cardiac ECG
Normal neurological examination and alert post-event state provide false reassurance against a serious condition
Drowning death of a family member not recognised as a cardiac red flag
Potassium and magnesium within normal limits may be incorrectly assumed to rule out all causes of QT prolongation

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Caitlin O'Brien is a 19-year-old right-handed woman and first-year university student who is brought to the emergency department by a fellow student after collapsing during a recreational run on the campus track. She was approximately 3 km into a 5-km run at moderate pace when she suddenly went pale, dropped to the ground, and was briefly unresponsive. The witness reports that her arms and legs jerked for approximately 10 to 15 seconds. She regained consciousness within 30 seconds and was immediately alert, asking 'Did I pass out again?' She did not bite her tongue, was not incontinent, and had no confusion beyond the initial seconds. She was able to walk with assistance after two minutes.

Ms. O'Brien discloses that this is her fourth such episode in four years, all occurring during physical exertion or strong emotional arousal:
- Episode 1 (age 15): Collapsed at a swim meet shortly after completing a 200-metre freestyle event; brief convulsive movements witnessed; taken to ED, loaded with levetiracetam, discharged with a diagnosis of 'exercise-induced seizure.'
- Episode 2 (age 16): Lost consciousness during a heated argument with a sibling; jerked briefly; attributed to the prior epilepsy diagnosis; levetiracetam dose was increased.
- Episode 3 (age 17): Near-syncope during a piano recital at peak emotional excitement; managed to sit down in time and did not fully lose consciousness.
- Episode 4 (today, age 19): Collapse during running, as described.

She has been maintained on levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily since age 15 and told she has epilepsy. She attends neurology clinic annually; her last visit 8 months ago documented 'well-controlled epilepsy on medication.' She has never had a cardiac evaluation, exercise ECG, or Holter monitor. Her parents note that her maternal uncle 'drowned' at age 28 in a swimming pool with lifeguards present; no toxicology or cardiac autopsy was performed.

On direct questioning, she describes episodes as preceded by a sudden awareness that her 'heart is pounding very hard,' then light-headedness, then loss of consciousness. There is no aura, no deja vu, no olfactory changes, no automatisms, and no post-ictal confusion. She does not feel sleepy after episodes. She has noticed occasional palpitations during intense exercise over the past year that resolve spontaneously. She denies chest pain, dyspnea at rest, or leg edema. She is a non-smoker, socially active, and on no medications other than levetiracetam.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration. No lateral tongue bite. No evidence of urinary incontinence. Small bruise over left knee from fall during today's episode. No post-ictal phase — patient was fully alert and oriented within approximately 30 seconds. She reports episodes are typically preceded by brief light-headedness or 'heart pounding,' not by aura, olfactory changes, or deja vu.
